title: Tested on mushrooms, an AI model shows potential for detecting crop stress with far fewer computations
description: A new artificial intelligence (AI) model can detect stress in agricultural crops using a nondestructive imaging technique, allowing changes in crop health to be monitored over time. Developed by a team of researchers at Penn State, the new model shows promise for accurately detecting crop stress caused by drought, disease, nutrient deficiency and other causes while using less computing power than some existing AI methods.

title: Two thirds of Swiss teenagers turn to chatbots for answers
description:
Swiss teenagers report spending about as much time online as they did in 2022. What they do there is changing fast. In 2026, 66% said they regularly used artificial intelligence to look up information, up from 22% two years earlier. Chatbots now rank third for finding things out, behind search engines and messaging apps and ahead of social networks.
Photo by fauxels on Pexels.com
The 2026 JAMES study, which analysed responses from 1,088 pupils aged 12 to 19 across Switzerland’s three main language regions, puts the median time online at three hours on a weekday and four hours and 50 minutes on a weekend day. Regular use of AI for entertainment rose too, from 5% to 21%.
A search engine offers links. A chatbot can make following them seem unnecessary. That is convenient when the answer is right, and troublesome when it is wrong. For news publishers there is a further problem. A chatbot can draw on their reporting and satisfy a reader’s curiosity before the reader sees the original article.
The spread of AI also exposes a change in who can afford what online. Some 99% of teenagers have a smartphone of their own, and ownership shows no statistically significant difference by family circumstances. Better-off households, however, are more likely to pay for AI tools, streaming services and newspapers. Teenagers from different backgrounds use AI about as often, according to the study. That leaves open the question of whether they get the same tools or the same quality of answers.
Regarding social media, the old favourites have held up. WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat lead the list of favourite apps. Teenagers use messaging apps and social networks chiefly to chat and to look at or react to other people’s posts. They publish their own less often. The categories themselves are getting harder to distinguish. WhatsApp lets users share updates with a wider circle, while Snapchat offers a public video feed.
For schools, the change in how pupils find information matters. Checking a chatbot’s answer means knowing where else to look and having access to sources worth checking. The authors suggest that school subscriptions and libraries could help give pupils access to resources their families might not buy. A lesson could start with a chatbot’s answer and ask pupils to trace a claim back to its source, then see whether the source says what the chatbot says it does. Swiss teenagers have taken to asking machines for answers quickly. Learning when to ask for evidence may take a little longer.
